Article Title: Meet the Humanoid Robot winning hearts in China after running 100 meter in less than 10 seconds; faster than any men's world record
Article Text:
Image courtesy: South China Morning Post

Rivalry with Honor’s lightning

Strategic industry for China

Global participation

A Chinese humanoid robot named Tiangong Ultra has captured global attention after running 100 metres in 9.39 seconds, faster than Usain Bolt’s men’s world record of 9.58 seconds, according to a report by Reuters. Developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, Tiangong Ultra won its preliminary heat at the second edition of the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, overtaking rival robot Lightning near the finish line.Lightning, built by smartphone maker Honor, finished close behind in 9.47 seconds, also faster than Bolt’s record set at the 2009 World Athletics Championships in Berlin. Earlier tests showed Lightning clocking 9.32 seconds, reaching a peak speed of 14.5 metres per second. Despite their speed, both robots lacked Bolt’s finesse — Tiangong stumbled into the sidelines, while Lightning collapsed and had to be carried away on a stretcher.Rapid progress since last yearThe results mark a dramatic leap from last year’s inaugural games, when Tiangong Ultra won the 100m in 21.50 seconds. Tiangong also made history by winning the world’s first humanoid half‑marathon in Beijing in 2025. Lightning, meanwhile, claimed this year’s half‑marathon title in 50 minutes and 26 seconds, faster than the pace of the elite men’s human world record.The 100m sprint is one of 51 events at the games, which also feature football, dancing, and industrial‑task contests. China has designated humanoid robots as a strategic emerging industry, betting that advances in AI and hardware will accelerate their adoption in manufacturing, logistics, and consumer applications. Investor enthusiasm is evident: shares of Unitree, China’s best‑known humanoid robot maker, surged more than fivefold in their Shanghai debut this week, giving the company a market value of about $50 billion.This year’s games, held at Beijing’s National Speed Skating Oval, have drawn 2,056 robots from 666 teams across 16 countries and six continents, a sharp increase from 280 teams last year.
Article Summary: Tiangong Ultra ran 100m in 9.39 seconds, faster than Usain Bolt’s world record of 9.58 seconds. It overtook rival robot Lightning, built by smartphone maker Honor, in the final. China has designated humanoid robots as a strategic emerging industry, betting that advances in AI will accelerate their adoption.

Article Title: After targeting water infrastructure in US, report claims Iran-linked hackers behind cyber attack on power plant in UK
Article Text:
Representative image

Iran demonstrating cyber capabilities

Hackers affiliated with the Iranian regime have allegedly conducted a cyberattack that forced a small-scale British power generation unit to shut down for four days last month. The incident is believed to represent the UK’s first recorded cyberattack targeting an energy generation asset. The breach coincided with a coordinated series of cyber incursions against water utility infrastructure across 12 US states. First reported by The Telegraph, British authorities confirmed that the incident never compromised the integrity of the wider national power grid or triggered electricity blackouts.As per UK energy minister Michael Shanks, the unit involved was small compared to conventional central power stations. Shanks added that both the generator operator and the government treated the security breach with complete seriousness.The UK power network incorporates thousands of small-scale distributed generation sites, primarily consisting of gas-powered units designed to fire up and provide temporary supply for only a few hours each week during peak demand.Due to operational security protocols, neither government ministers nor the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which oversees critical national infrastructure defense, has disclosed the exact identity or location of the affected facility, emphasizing that the breach did not hit critical base-load assets.Security analysts cited in The Telegraph noted that the attack may have been executed as a demonstration of technical capability, aimed at proving that cyber units tied to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) could penetrate British energy systems and shut down physical infrastructure. While Western cybersecurity agencies have maintained heightened alert levels for state-backed attacks following regional conflicts involving the US, direct cyber intrusions against UK power assets have historically been rare.In response to the incident, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) contacted commercial energy operators across Britain to advise them on emerging threat vectors.Meanwhile, the National Cyber Security Centre issued a wider warning regarding a growing wave of cyber operations launched by state and non-state actors against British organisations, urging all operators to review defensive setups and implement hardening protocols.
Article Summary: The incident is believed to represent the UK’s first recorded cyberattack targeting an energy generation asset. The breach coincided with a coordinated series of cyber incursions against water utility infrastructure across 12 US states. The UK power network incorporates thousands of small-scale distributed generation sites.

Article Title: Read memo that Zohran Mamdani's team sent to 'upset' New Yorkers who say we do not get how you will tax our million-dollar homes
Article Text:
Why New York homeowners are upset

What the memo clarifies

Extended deadline for appeals

Read the complete memo here:

Chair Gale Brewer, Chair Linda Lee, and Members of the City Council,

My name is Richard Lee, and I am the Commissioner of the

New York City Department of Finance

(DOF).

Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony regarding the implementation of the surcharge on non-primary residence properties, commonly referred to as a "pied-a-terre."

I understand the Council's interest in holding this hearing to discuss the implementation of this surcharge. The public understandably has a range of questions about this surcharge and the manner in which it has been implemented. I have been engaged with members of your team, and directly with many of you, to ensure that New Yorkers have the information that they need. I would have welcomed the opportunity to appear in person and field your questions directly, but the pending and active litigation precludes me from doing so.

The Administration requested that the City Council postpone the hearing to the near future but the Council declined. In the meantime, I appreciate the opportunity to address some of those questions in my written testimony.

First, let me walk through the steps that led to implementation of the surcharge — from the passage of the state legislation authorizing the surcharge, through the rule-making process, to the posting of a supplemental roll and transmission of initial determination letters.

On May 28, 2026, as part of the State's 2026/2027 budget legislation, the State enacted part HH of chapter 59 of 2026, which authorized this surcharge on certain high-value New York City residential properties that are not used as a primary residence. The law was enacted with support from the Mayor and his Administration to help close a significant budget gap. The statutory provisions relating to this surcharge can be found in Article 30-C of the New York State Tax Law and Chapter 32 of Title 11 of the City's Administrative Code.

As with all revenue collected by DOF, these funds help keep the City running. The revenue DOF collects supports essential services that New Yorkers rely on every day, from educating our children in public schools and maintaining our parks to ensuring our streets are clean and our trash is collected.

DOF took steps to ensure the surcharge would be implemented through a transparent, consistent, and fair process that is legally compliant.

On June 9, 2026, DOF published proposed rules outlining how the new surcharge would be administered and applied. As part of the rulemaking process, property owners and other members of the public had an opportunity to submit written feedback, provide testimony, and raise questions or concerns at a public hearing held on July 9, 2026.

DOF reviewed the feedback that it received through the notice-and-comment process, made appropriate adjustments to the rule text, and promulgated the final rules necessary to implement the surcharge.

These rules were thereafter adopted on July 14, 2026 and took effect immediately. After adopting these rules, DOF moved forward with implementing the surcharge and, as required by law, published a supplemental roll on its website.

Each year, the City publishes real property market values and assessed values for all taxable property through its annual assessment roll. The purpose of the assessment roll is to provide the public with notice about every property subject to real property taxation throughout the five boroughs, the assessed and market values associated with such property, and certain information necessary to identify the property and its ownership.

Both the Real Property Tax Law and the City Charter require the City to publish an assessment roll of taxable property in this manner, and assessment rolls have been required to be published annually for well over a century. In accordance with the City Charter, DOF publishes the tentative assessment roll for the upcoming fiscal year every January. Upon publication of this tentative assessment roll, property owners may challenge certain assessment-related matters, including by making a filing with the City's independent Tax Commission.

On the date that the Tax Commission is required to render final determinations on these challenges—May 25 of each year—DOF releases its final assessment roll.

The City's assessment roll is highly accessible to the public, and it has been for many years. Any suggestion to the contrary is incorrect. For example, this property data has been publicly available as a fully searchable database on both the DOF website and NYC Open Data.

DOF's online archives include assessment roll data dating back to fiscal year 2009.

Many data elements included on the roll relating to property ownership are culled from land records and have also long been available through DOF's Automated City Register Information System (ACRIS). The City has published assessment rolls and made them available for public examination, in various forms, for over a hundred years.

Before internet accessibility, the City's assessment rolls and land records were made available for review in person at government offices.

Section 11-3205 of the Administrative Code, part of the statutory framework governing the surcharge, requires the City to administer and enforce the surcharge "to the greatest extent practicable . . . in the same manner used to administer and enforce real property taxes," and requires the publication of corresponding property valuation information on a roll.

The law authorizing the surcharge was adopted after the assessment roll for fiscal year 2026-2027 had already been published.

As a result, the law governing the surcharge required the City to release a supplemental mid-cycle roll for the 2026-2027 tax year in order for the surcharge to be administered. Stated differently, for the 2026-2027 fiscal year only, DOF published a new assessment roll mid-year — the July 2026 supplemental roll.

This largely involved republishing data from the May 2026 final assessment roll.

DOF published the required supplemental roll on July 24,2026. The supplemental roll includes relevant property valuation information, and certain descriptive information regarding all property that meets the surcharge statute's definition of "covered property." The universe of properties considered "covered property" for purposes of the law is much broader than the properties that were sent initial determination letters, as explained below, or that will eventually be subject to the surcharge.

In light of this, it is important to emphasize what the supplemental roll does not do. The supplemental roll does not establish which properties are subject to the surcharge. It generally includes certain information to identify such properties and their ownership. Like the assessment roll, publication of the supplemental roll provides a basis for property owners to challenge the value of their properties.

The law also requires DOF to send initial determination letters to property owners whose properties may be subject to the surcharge and whose primary residency could not be confirmed based on the information available to the agency, as described in DOF rules.

Only a very small subset of the population of properties that were listed on the supplemental roll received an initial determination letter, about 17,000 homes out of a total of approximately 960,000 listed homes.

The surcharge only applies to those class one properties —which typically include one to three family homes — with market values greater than or equal to $5,000,000 and cooperative and condominium dwelling units with market values greater than or equal to $1,000,000.

Some properties that would have otherwise received an initial determination letter did not ultimately receive one because DOF already possessed data that sufficiently demonstrated that the property was used as a primary residence and was therefore not subject to the surcharge. For example, homeowners who affirmatively established primary residency with DOF already for the 2026-2027 fiscal year, such as homeowners who receive the Senior Citizens Homeowners' Exemption (SCHE), or the Disabled Homeowners' Exemption (DHE), and therefore have provided proof of residency as well as proof of income for eligibility, did not receive this initial determination letter.

One of the most important aspects of this procedure is that this initial determination is not a tax bill. These notices simply inform property owners that, based on the information currently available to DOF, their property may be subject to the new surcharge. This is an initial determination, not a final one.

Property owners who believe their property should not be subject to the surcharge have an opportunity to submit proof the property is used as a primary residence.

This process allows property owners to provide information that is readily available to the owners but may not be reflected in DOF's records. Through this process, property owners can provide DOF with the information DOF needs to make accurate determinations regarding surcharge eligibility before the surcharge is applied.

For example, a primary homeowner can submit their driver's license as proof of primary residency.

Property owners can alternatively challenge DOF's initial determination directly with the Tax Commission if they are also challenging their market value. For the 2026-2027 tax year, they have until March 2027 to do so.

In implementing the surcharge, we have focused on providing transparency about which properties may be affected and ensuring homeowners have a straightforward way to resolve their status. We recognize that homeowners need clear information and meaningful support as they navigate the process.

That is why DOF has prioritized direct assistance and outreach.

DOF has been engaging homeowners and plans to further conduct proactive outreach at senior centers, community meetings, and other public forums; provide information through our dedicated website, nyc.gov/npsurcharge, and 311; and continue to work directly with co-op and condominium boards, property managers and building representatives to share information with residents.

Where contact information for a property owner is available, we are also reaching out directly to homeowners who received notices to answer questions and provide guidance on the initial determination appeals process.

In addition, we are partnering with elected officials, community leaders and constituent services staff to distribute accurate information and connect homeowners with available resources.

We have also announced an extension through September 18, 2026 for homeowners to submit appeals of initial determinations.

We believe these efforts reflect the Administration's commitment to ensure that every potentially affected homeowner understands the process, knows where to turn for support and has a fair opportunity to challenge a DOF initial determination.

I understand there are concerns regarding this surcharge. I also understand that there are individuals who received an initial determination letter who may not ultimately owe the surcharge.

That is exactly why DOF has expanded its customer service and extended the deadline for property owners to challenge initial determinations. DOF is working directly with building managers, elected officials, and homeowners to answer questions and make the process as straightforward as possible.

Whenever government implements a new law affecting thousands of property owners, questions inevitably arise. Government should communicate clearly and effectively about new policies, and DOF is committed to doing that, not just with respect to this law, but across all aspects of DOF's work.

DOF is committed to ensuring that this surcharge is only applied to those properties thatare subject to the surcharge under the law. DOF is focused on making sure every homeowner has the information they need to understand the key contours of the law and to determine whether they are subject to the surcharge.

DOF's role is to administer and implement the law. As implementation moves forward, DOF has continued to engage with elected officials, respond to constituent concerns, and provide updates and guidance to help New Yorkers navigate the process.

We welcome continued feedback from the City Council and all stakeholders as we work to administer this new law with fairness, consistency, and clarity. I am prepared and would welcome the opportunity to testify after August 31.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani ’s administration chose not to attend Tuesday’s (August 25) City Council hearing on the rollout of the pied‑à‑terre tax, instead submitting a detailed written memo seen by Business Insider. Finance Commissioner Richard Lee explained that ongoing litigation prevented him from appearing in person, but emphasised that the Department of Finance (DOF) is committed to transparency and fairness in implementing the surcharge.The levy, passed in May, imposes a progressive surcharge on non‑primary residences valued at least $5 million, and condos or co‑ops worth $1 million or more. In late July, DOF sent letters to 17,000 addresses and published valuations for nearly 960,000 properties. Many residents said they mistakenly received letters for their primary homes, while others raised privacy concerns over the release of property records.Lee’s memo stressed that the supplemental roll does not establish which properties are subject to the surcharge, but instead provides a basis for owners to challenge valuations. He noted that only a small subset of properties received initial determination letters and that these notices are not tax bills.Homeowners can submit proof of primary residency — such as a driver’s license — to avoid the surcharge.To ease concerns, DOF extended the deadline for appeals to September 18, 2026. The city has also hired two dozen staffers to assist residents and is conducting outreach through senior centers, community meetings, and 311.
Article Summary: Richard Lee is commissioner of the New York City Department of Finance. Lee: "The public understandably has a range of questions about this surcharge and the manner in which it has been implemented" "I would have welcomed the opportunity to appear in person and field your questions directly," he says.

Article Title: Godfather of AI Yann Lecun wants AI models to upgrade from writing his essays to solving this 'big bedroom problem'
Article Text:
Yann Lecun to Amazon's Jitendra Malik: I don't agree with your definition

AI 'godfather' leaves Meta after 12 years

Meta's former Chief AI scientist who is also popularly regarded as the Godfather of AI, Yann Lecun, wants AI models to do lots more. In a post on X, formerly Twitter Lecun said that he wants LLMs (Large Language Models) to do a lot more including physical work. He made the comment while replying to Paul Graham. "Someone asked what I'd do if I were 17. I'd learn how to build LLMs from scratch, and then train ones as powerful as I could with whatever hardware I could get access to," wrote Graham in a post on X.To this Lecun replied, "I would try to figure out why LLMs can write my essays but not clean my bedroom. Then I would study topics in college and grad school that could help solve that problem. I'll figure out a set of methods and architectures beyond LLMs that can quickly learn to perform physical tasks as efficiently as humans and animals. That last item is also what I would if I were 30, 40, 50, or 66 years old."In a similar context he also replied to his former colleague at Meta Jitendra Malik, who last month left the Facebook-parent to join Amazon's robotics division. Malik wrote, "Scientific terms should have precision.If we use the terms VLM, VLA, WAM in an indiscriminate fashion, as is becoming common in robotics, we are not helping clarity in communication. Let's keep the historical origins of these terms in mind. VLMs arose as multimodal extensions of LLMs-the training was for tasks like VQA (VIsual Question Answering). These capture the static semantics of the scene behind an image. No dynamics. World Models (e.g.@ylecun) Ha & Schmidhuber 2018) on the other hand are primarily dynamics models, which go back to control theory -1960 (Bellman, Kalman etc.) This makes them natural for robotics planning / policies- I am in a state s, what action a should I perform to get to state s'. In classical control, these models were written down a priori by modeling the physics of the system; today we think of them as learned neural networks trained from temporal data e.g. video, robot trajectories. But the concept is the same. We shouldn't mix this concept with VLMs."Amazon exec tagged Yann Lecun in his post. Lecun disagreed with him on his views on LLMs, VLMs and robotics. He said that he does not agree with Malik's definition. "Exactly. We also should not confuse world models, as per your definition, with video prediction or video generation models. Understanding the dynamics of a system in order to control it is not the same as producing cute videos," wrote Lecun.For those unaware, Yann LeCun is a French-American computer scientist widely known as one of the Godfathers of AI. He won the 2018 Turing Award for deep learning, created convolutional neural networks (CNNs), served as Meta's Chief AI Scientist, and is a professor at New York University. In November 2025, Leun announced his planned departure from Meta, the company he has been part of for twelve years. "As many of you have heard through rumours or recent media articles, I am planning to leave Meta after 12 years: 5 years as founding director of FAIR and 7 years as Chief AI Scientist," he wrote. "The impact of FAIR on the company, on the field of AI, on the tech community, and on the wider world has been spectacular," he added.
Article Summary: AI 'godfather' leaves Meta after 12 years as Chief AI Scientist. Yann Lecun wants LLMs (Large Language Models) to do a lot more including physical work. He also replied to his former colleague at Meta Jitendra Malik, who last month left the Facebook-parent to join Amazon's robotics division.

Article Title: Apple’s first foldable iPhone may take a step back from using standard feature for authentication
Article Text:
Apple foldable iPhone may launch at $2,000

Apple’s first foldable iPhone: Key hardware omissions but premium pricing

Apple is likely gearing up to introduce its first-ever foldable iPhone at an upcoming launch event targeted on or around September 9, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman has said, revealing some of the key details which indicate that the phone may compromise on certain standard premium features, notably swapping facial recognition for older biometric authentication.According to Gurman, rather than featuring the company's established Face ID system, the foldable design relies on Touch ID for user authentication. While returning to fingerprint scanning may feel like a step backward to some modern smartphone owners, many users remain comfortable with Touch ID across current Mac computers and iPads, he said.The foldable iPhone will function as an ultra-premium flagship with retail pricing expected to exceed $2,000. However, early impressions highlight a significant hardware omission, Gurman said.Despite excelling as an expanded camera viewfinder, the initial model lacks a telephoto camera for optical zoom. Given that the target audience willing to pay more than $2,000 closely overlaps with users demanding top-tier camera versatility, omitting advanced zoom could impact early sales.Citing testers who have handled the hardware, Gurman said that the device fits comfortably into pockets, highlighting the durability and feel of the sophisticated hinge system alongside new iPad-style multitasking interfaces optimized for the large internal screen.The form factor enables users to switch between regular single-handed tasks, such as texting or making quick phone calls, and an expansive display suited for video streaming, mobile gaming and other work.Increased consumer awareness could simultaneously benefit Android manufacturers like Samsung and Google, whose offerings feature larger screens and mature folding hardware that some buyers may view as higher-tier alternatives.
Article Summary: The foldable iPhone will function as an ultra-premium flagship with retail pricing expected to exceed $2,000. The initial model lacks a telephoto camera for optical zoom. The device fits comfortably into pockets, highlighting the durability and feel of the hinge system alongside new iPad-style multitasking interfaces.

Article Title: Slack Code puts AI coding agents in the group chat, and everyone gets to watch
Article Text:
Slack Code puts Claude, Devin, Copilot and ChatGPT into shared channels where the whole team can watch, steer and approve the work before it ships.

Slack says writing code stopped being the hard part

Slack has launched Slack Code, a product that drags AI coding agents out of private terminals and into shared channels where the whole team can follow along. Tag an agent like Anthropic's Claude, Cognition's Devin, GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT or Vercel's agent from any conversation, and it spins up a project-specific code channel to take on the job. That channel carries its own tabs for the conversation, the plan, the code diffs and a live HTML preview of what the agent built. Once the task is finished, the channel archives itself and leaves behind a searchable audit log.The feature went live on August 20 and works on every Slack plan, including free ones. The catch is that access to each partner agent is bought separately, which tells you exactly where Salesforce expects the money to sit. Slack calls the idea "multiplayer AI," and the pitch is that a product manager, a designer and an engineer can all steer the same agent without anyone opening a terminal."Code is no longer the bottleneck," Rob Seaman, Slack's interim CEO, said in a press briefing. "Ideas, taste, judgment, craft, those are the things that are the bottleneck." Cognition backed the velocity claim with its own numbers, with president of new enterprise Jeff Wang saying merged pull requests jumped tenfold in recent months while headcount rose about 40 percent.The obvious worry is AI slop arriving at scale. Slack VP of product Katie Steigman argues visibility is the fix rather than the problem, since colleagues can see your intent and tell you the output is weak before it ships. Her own habit is to tag an engineer on every pull request she opens.On security, agents inherit the permissions of whoever invokes them. Seaman was blunt that there are no god permissions or bot-level access, and that a code channel only hands the agent context from the conversation that triggered it. Merging to production still needs human sign-off inside the channel.Slack is also shipping agent DMs, a new Agents tab with live status and a stop button, and an Add to Slack flow for agents built on Lovable, n8n and LangChain. The code channel APIs open to outside developers later, with marketing and legal work named as the next targets.
Article Summary: Slack has launched Slack Code, a product that drags AI coding agents into shared channels. The whole team can watch, steer and approve the work before it ships. Slack calls the idea "multiplayer AI," and the pitch is that a product manager, a designer and an engineer can all steer the same agent.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Jack Dorsey: “Everyone has an idea. But it’s really about executing the idea and…” - simple lesson about taking the first step
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Jack Dorsey

“Everyone has an idea. But it’s really about executing the idea and attracting other people to help you work on the idea.”

What Jack Dorsey meant by the quote

Why having an idea is only the beginning

The role of other people in turning ideas into reality

Jack Dorsey’s early interest in technology

How Dorsey turned a simple payment idea into Square

Execution means testing an idea against reality

Why collaboration can change the original idea

The difference between an idea and a working product

What Dorsey’s quote means for everyday projects

Why the quote remains relevant

Lessons learnt from Jack Dorsey’s quote

An idea needs action to become useful.

You do not have to build everything alone.

Execution reveals what an idea is missing.

The first version does not need to be perfect.

Feedback can make an idea stronger.

Collaboration brings skills and perspectives you may lack.

Simple ideas can require complex execution.

Adaptability is part of turning an idea into reality.

An idea can arrive in a few seconds. It might come while solving a problem at work, talking with a friend, using a product or simply wondering whether something could be done differently. Most people have ideas from time to time, but very few ever turn them into something real. The difference is rarely just about having a clever thought. An idea needs time, effort, testing and, in many cases, other people who can bring skills that the original creator does not have. That is the thinking behind a well-known observation from Jack Dorsey, the co-founder of Twitter and Square. The quote points to a simple distinction: thinking of something is only the beginning. What follows is the harder process of making it work.Dorsey’s point is not that ideas have little value. An original idea can provide the direction for a product, business or project. But an idea remains theoretical until someone starts making decisions about how it could work in practice.Execution is where those decisions begin. A person has to decide what to build first, what can be left out, what resources are needed and how the idea should change when reality does not match the original plan.The second part of the quote is just as important. Dorsey refers to attracting other people to work on the idea, recognising that large projects rarely depend on one person alone. Different people may bring technical knowledge, design skills, business experience, funding, contacts or an understanding of customers.Ideas are easy to discuss because they have no practical limitations yet. Once someone tries to build one, those limitations become visible.A product may cost more than expected. A technical problem may force a redesign. Customers may not respond as anticipated. Something that seemed essential might turn out to be unnecessary.This is why execution can change an idea rather than simply reproduce it. The original concept provides a starting point, while the process of building reveals what actually works.A founder may have the initial concept, but that does not mean they possess every skill needed to develop it.A software project might require programmers, designers, product managers and people who understand the market. A physical product could need engineers, manufacturers and distributors. Even a small personal project can become easier when someone else brings knowledge or experience that the creator lacks.Dorsey’s wording about “attracting” people also suggests that collaboration cannot simply be assumed. Others need to understand the purpose of the project and see a reason to contribute.Dorsey was born in St Louis, Missouri, in 1976 and developed an interest in computers while growing up. He became particularly interested in communication and dispatch systems, including the way information could be shared quickly between people working in different locations.That interest later became relevant to the technology projects he pursued. He studied at the Missouri University of Science and Technology before attending New York University, although he left university without completing his degree. He subsequently worked as a programmer and became involved with software relating to dispatch and real-time communication.His early career was not built around a single grand plan. Instead, several interests gradually came together around software, communication and the movement of information.Dorsey later applied his interest in communication and technology to a very different problem.In 2009, he co-founded Square with Jim McKelvey. The company developed a small card reader that could connect to a mobile device, allowing businesses and individuals to accept card payments without relying on traditional payment terminals.The device looked simple, but the system behind it was not. Payment technology involves security, financial regulations, software, hardware and relationships with financial institutions.Square eventually expanded beyond its original product into a broader range of financial services. The company changed its corporate name to Block in 2021.The contrast between Twitter and Square is useful when considering Dorsey’s quote. The initial concepts for both companies could be explained relatively simply. Building businesses around those concepts required considerably more work and the involvement of many other people.Execution is often treated as simply completing a plan. In practice, it can mean discovering that the original plan needs to change.A prototype may reveal a technical problem. Early customers may ask for something unexpected. A product that looks useful may prove difficult to operate at scale. These experiences provide information that cannot always be gained through planning alone. That is why the first version of a product does not have to be perfect. It can serve as a way of finding out what works, what does not and what needs to be changed before more resources are committed.Bringing other people into a project introduces different perspectives.A programmer might identify a technical limitation that the founder had overlooked. A designer might notice that the product is difficult to understand. Someone working with customers might discover that the problem being solved is slightly different from what the team originally assumed.These disagreements can be useful when they are handled constructively. The final product may therefore contain ideas that were not present in the original concept. That does not necessarily mean the initial idea failed. It can mean the idea developed as more information became available.There is a natural temptation to focus on the moment an idea is conceived. It feels like the creative part, and it can be exciting to imagine what something might become. The less visible work comes afterwards. Someone has to build the first version, find out whether people want it, correct mistakes and keep improving it. If the project grows, more people become involved and the work becomes divided across different areas.At that stage, the original idea is still important, but it is no longer the whole project.The principle does not apply only to technology companies or entrepreneurs. Someone may have an idea for improving a process at work, starting a community project, creating a small business or learning a new skill. The same question eventually appears: what is the first practical step?It may be as simple as making a prototype, speaking to potential users, writing down the requirements or finding someone with the missing expertise. Starting small can also make an idea easier to evaluate. Instead of trying to prove that the entire concept will work, a person can test one part of it.Ideas have become easier to share, but turning them into functioning products, businesses or projects still takes practical work.Dorsey’s experience reflects that gap. Twitter began with a relatively simple communication concept, while Square started with a straightforward approach to accepting card payments. Both eventually required large teams and complex systems.His quote captures the distinction in simple terms. Having an idea is common. Making it work requires execution, and building something substantial often requires other people willing to take part in the process.
Article Summary: Jack Dorsey is the co-founder of Twitter and Square. He said: ‘It’s really about executing the idea and attracting other people to help you work on the idea’ An idea needs time, effort, testing and other people who can bring skills that the original creator does not have.

Article Title: Marvel's Spider-Man: Brand New Day faces AI controversy
Article Text:
Marvel's $2 billion Spider-Man hit is facing AI backlash over one artbook image

Two taxis warping into each other and a fire escape twisting into stairs that go nowhere: the telltale signs fans spotted in "Big City, Little Spider"

Marvel's AI problem did not start with this artbook

Spider-Man: Brand New Day has crossed $2 billion worldwide. It opened to $360 million in North America, the biggest domestic opening weekend in history, and roughly $932 million globally, second only to Avengers: Endgame. By every commercial measure, this is the most successful thing Marvel Studios has done in years. And now it has an AI problem, sitting inside a $50 hardcover that fans have already bought."The Art of Spider-Man: Brand New Day" reached shelves on August 18, a 208-page collector's book, and readers working through it have flagged one piece of concept art that looks machine-generated. The image is titled "Big City, Little Spider" and credited to concept artist Scott McInnes. At a glance it is an ordinary New York street, all yellow cabs and walk-up buildings. Zoom in and it falls apart. Two taxis heading in opposite directions fuse into each other mid-frame. A fire escape on the left twists into stairs that go nowhere. Traffic lights sit at strange angles. Windows land where no working artist would put them.The find surfaced through The Artbook Collector, was reported by The Direct, and spread across X, Reddit and ResetEra within hours.The complaint is specific rather than abstract. A film clearing $2 billion apparently could not pay a human to draw a taxi correctly. Readers who went through the rest of the book say the other pages look clean, which suggests one image slipped past quality control rather than a pattern running through the collection.McInnes has a serious blockbuster résumé, including Morbius, The Fantastic Four: First Steps, Guardians of the Galaxy, Andor, Barbie and Wonka. That history is part of why the reaction has been so sharp.The timing helps nobody. Marvel cut a large chunk of its visual development team months ago, the people who build a film's look before cameras roll. Fans drew their own conclusions then. Secret Invasion's AI-assisted title sequence from 2023 still gets brought up. DC recently pulled a Supergirl behind-the-scenes video after viewers spotted AI concept art of Jason Momoa's Lobo.Marvel has not commented. Buyers found out after paying.
Article Summary: Marvel's $2 billion Spider-Man hit is facing AI backlash over one artbook image. The image is titled "Big City, Little Spider" and credited to concept artist Scott McInnes. Two taxis warping into each other and a fire escape twisting into stairs that go nowhere.

Article Title: In 2023, Canadian wildfires cut solar power generation by 6.38 TWh across North America and Europe, causing an estimated $1.9 billion loss
Article Text:
Representative Image

How Canadian wildfire smoke affected solar power generation

Other factors affecting solar power generation

Wildfires can also damage solar panels and equipment

Wildfires may be adversely affecting solar power generation worldwide. According to a recent study published in Nature, smoke from the Canadian wildfires in 2023 reduced solar electricity generation across North America and Europe by an estimated 6.38 terawatt-hours (TWh) over five months. The researchers estimated that the reduction amounted to about 2.8% of the solar electricity generated across the two regions during that period.The report also estimated that the decline in solar generation caused an economic loss of about $1.9 billion and was associated with about 2.1 megatons of CO2 emissions. Researchers attributed the drop to smoke and airborne particles from the wildfires that blocked or scattered sunlight before it could reach solar panels, though they noted significant uncertainty around the estimates.The 2023 Canadian wildfire season produced large amounts of smoke that travelled across North America and reached parts of Europe. The researchers modelled the atmospheric effects of the wildfire emissions over five months to estimate their impact on solar electricity generation.Sunlight is absorbed and scattered by particles in the atmosphere. This results in less sunlight reaching the solar panels, and installations producing less electricity even if the panels themselves are not directly affected by fire.The findings also show how the effects of wildfires can extend beyond areas immediately surrounding the fires. Solar farms, commercial installations and rooftop systems can all be affected when smoke moves through the atmosphere above them.Wildfire smoke is not the only source of air pollution that decreases the productivity of solar panel arrays. Pollution particles (particulate matter) released into the air by automobiles and coal-burning electrical generators may decrease how much sunlight enters your solar array.Dust can affect panels in different ways by settling directly on the panel surface . Dust accumulation from construction and mining activities can reduce electricity generation if panels are not cleaned.Improved solar-power forecasting can help grid operators prepare for generation changes caused by smoke. More accurate forecasts can help operators anticipate declines in solar output and arrange alternative electricity sources to maintain the balance between supply and demand.According to Cornell University, researchers studied a machine learning model for predicting solar energy production during certain extreme wildfire smoke OPS events in 2025. Researchers indicated that the model has more detail and accuracy than the New York grid operator's forecasts.Emissions from automobiles and factories are a source of atmospheric pollution. These can be reduced with improved dust management at solar farms. This will limit the effects of pollution on the farms’ ability to generate electricity.Wildfire smoke can affect solar generation without physically damaging an installation, but fires can also directly threaten solar farms. The U.S. Department of Energy has identified wildfire damage as a risk to photovoltaic systems, including potential damage to panels and components used to operate them.A solar farm owned by a French company Luxel was affected by a wildfire last month. The fire broke out in southern France in July 2026. About 100 of the 43,500 panels and some cables were damaged in the blaze, while the transformers and inverters were not harmed.Vegetation management around the site helped limit the fire's reach. Luxel said that regular clearing work, including a 50-meter perimeter around the fences, helped prevent flames from reaching most of the installation.The US Department of Energy recommends maintaining defensible space around solar installations in areas exposed to wildfire risk. Its measures include managing vegetation, paving areas around critical equipment, placing important electrical components in fire-resistant containers, maintaining access for firefighters and keeping an updated wildfire emergency-response plan.The Canadian wildfire study illustrates how fires can affect solar power production without reaching a solar energy facility, and physical damage to infrastructure is an additional risk to facilities built in wildland-urban interface areas.
Article Summary: Smoke from the Canadian wildfires in 2023 reduced solar electricity generation across North America and Europe by an estimated 6.38 terawatt-hours. The decline in solar generation caused an economic loss of about $1.9 billion and was associated with about 2.1 megatons of CO2 emissions. Researchers attributed the drop to smoke and airborne particles from the wildfires.

Article Title: Startup founded by three Harvard dropouts that tech investors warned of saying 'don’t back kids in chips' is pulling talent from Nvidia; engineer says ...
Article Text:
Etched co-founders Robert Wachen, Gavin Uberti and Chris Zhu. (Image source: WSJ)

Investors once warned ‘Don’t back the kids in chips’

Etched is hiring from Nvidia

A chip startup once viewed by investors as too inexperienced to take on the semiconductor industry is now pulling engineers from Nvidia and other major chip companies, as it moves closer to becoming a serious player in AI hardware. Etched, founded by three 24-year-old Harvard dropouts, has signed quantitative-trading firm Jane Street as its first customer, booked more than $1 billion in orders and started shipping its AI chips. The hiring trend has also surprised some of its new employees. Former Nvidia systems engineer Anthony Gamerman said he kept hearing about colleagues leaving Nvidia for Etched. “One leaves, and then another one, you hear a couple weeks later, and you go, ‘Whoa, I can’t believe so-and-so is heading over to Etched,’” he said.Etched was started by Robert Wachen, Gavin Uberti and Chris Zhu, who are all 24 years old. The company initially struggled to attract investors because of the founders' limited experience in semiconductor hardware.Sonya Huang, a general partner at Sequoia Capital, described the concern among investors at the time. “Among tech investors, the prevailing wisdom was ‘don’t back the kids in chips,’” Huang said.She added that investors believed young founders could succeed in internet businesses but faced much bigger challenges when building semiconductor hardware.Etched has since raised nearly $2 billion, including a new $700 million funding round led by Jane Street that values the company at $21 billion.The startup has built a team with significant semiconductor experience. Around 15% of its roughly 400 employees previously worked at Nvidia, according to Etched. The company has also hired engineers from other established semiconductor firms.Brian Loiler, who spent nearly 23 years at Nvidia, joined Etched to work on its servers and racks. He has since helped recruit about a dozen Nvidia engineers to the startup, with some turning down counteroffers. Jimmy Daley, a former Nvidia vice president of data-center systems engineering who retired in July, is also an investor in Etched.The company has developed AI processors designed specifically for this workload. Its first customer is Jane Street, a quantitative trading firm that uses powerful computing systems to run trading models quickly. Etched says it has already started shipping its chips and took just 44 days to get its test chips running inference workloads after receiving them from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing.“We may be the only AI chip that was built by a startup that was successful on the first try,” Etched co-founder and president Robert Wachen said.
Article Summary: Etched, founded by three 24-year-old Harvard dropouts, has signed quantitative- trading firm Jane Street as its first customer. The company has booked more than $1 billion in orders and started shipping its AI chips. Around 15% of its roughly 400 employees previously worked at Nvidia.

Article Title: Nelco and Elveo join forces to deliver next-gen satellite solutions

Article Title: Judge accused of relying entirely on AI still protected from lawsuit, US court rules
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representation purposes only

What judicial immunity means in the case

Judges may still face other challenges

A US federal court has ruled that a judge accused of relying entirely on AI to make a court decision can still be protected by judicial immunity. This could mean that the judge cannot be sued over the alleged AI use. According to a report by Tom’s Hardware, the decision comes from Phillips v. Parlade, a case decided by US District Judge Gloria Navarro of the District of Nevada. The plaintiff, Phillips, argued that judicial immunity should not protect the state judge because she allegedly handed over her decision-making duties completely to AI.In the lawsuit, Phillips claimed that if the judge had delegated 100% of the decision-making to artificial intelligence, the resulting order could not be considered a judicial act based on the judge's own judgment.He also argued that such complete delegation meant the judge had acted outside her legal jurisdiction, which can be an exception to judicial immunity. Judge Navarro rejected those arguments.US judges generally have broad protection from civil lawsuits over actions taken in their judicial role. That protection can apply even when a judge is accused of making mistakes, acting with bad motives or going beyond their authority.Exceptions exist. That immunity may not apply when the judge acts in total absence of jurisdiction or when the act complained of is not a judicial act.Courts generally consider several factors when deciding whether an action is judicial. These include whether it is a normal part of a judge's duties, whether it happened in chambers, whether it involved a case before the judge and whether the judge was acting in an official capacity.In this case, the federal court found that issuing a decision in a pending case was clearly part of a judge's normal duties. Phillips also did not claim that the decision was made outside the judge's chambers or provide legal support for the argument that AI use placed the judge outside her jurisdiction.As a result, the court concluded that judicial immunity still applied and dismissed the lawsuit.The ruling, however, does not prevent litigants from challenging a judge's actions through other legal channels. According to the report, a person can appeal a decision through the state court system, seek other available legal remedies or file a disciplinary complaint against the judge.The case therefore leaves a key question open: “what legal or ethical rules should apply if a judge actually delegates judicial decision-making to an AI system?,” the report states.
Article Summary: US judges generally have broad protection from civil lawsuits over actions taken in their judicial role. That protection can apply even when a judge is accused of making mistakes, acting with bad motives or going beyond their authority. That immunity may not apply when the judge acts in total absence of jurisdiction or when the act complained of is not a judicial act.

Article Title: TagMango launches AI tools for courses, apps and websites

Article Title: After cutting hundreds of jobs, Disney to now cut employee benefits; says: In response to rising healthcare costs in the US, we are ...
Article Text:
Additional corporate programs and US headcount

Nationwide surge in corporate healthcare expenses

Following thousands of staff reductions, The Walt Disney Company is adjusting its corporate benefits package by curtailing healthcare coverage for employees’ working spouses as medical inflation across the US mounts. Beginning next year, the entertainment conglomerate will exclude spouses of US workers from company medical insurance plans if those spouses have access to healthcare coverage through their own employers, a Disney representative confirmed to Business Insider.“Like a growing number of large employers, we're making measured adjustments to our employee benefits in response to rising healthcare costs nationwide,” Disney stated in an official communication. The revised policy will not alter healthcare benefits for other dependent family members, nor does it impact dental or vision plans for spouses, the report added.Joshua Lavine, chief executive of insurance consultancy Capitol Benefits, characterized the decision as an unusually strict cost-cutting measure. Lavine pointed out that while many employers choose to reduce the financial subsidy provided for a spouse's plan, entirely eliminating access to coverage is uncommon.While spouses who are unemployed or whose workplaces offer no health benefits remain eligible for Disney's plan, Lavine cautioned that the policy shift could complicate continuous medical treatment for individuals undergoing long-term care.The benefit adjustment follows earlier reports that Disney plans to launch an employee stock-purchase initiative later in 2027, subject to necessary authorisations. As of September 2025, Disney employed approximately 172,000 workers across the US.The policy shift at Disney comes at a time when there is a steep price increase across the American employer-sponsored healthcare system. A report released by insurance brokerage Aon forecasts that employer medical spending will jump 9.5% next year, which represents the fourth straight year of near double-digit increases and extending a historic stretch of healthcare cost inflation.Other major employers are trimming benefits in response. Coffee giant Starbucks announced it will discontinue health insurance coverage for GLP-1 weight-loss drugs starting in October for eligible hourly and salaried staff who work at least 20 hours per week.A survey conducted this spring by Mercer indicated that almost half of US organisations with at least 500 workers plan to restructure their health plans next year through higher co-payments and deductibles. Beyond health plans, companies such as Zoom have scaled down paid parental leave policies, while Deloitte announced reductions covering paid time off, pension contributions, fertility funding and parental leave for segments of its US workforce beginning in January.
Article Summary: The Walt Disney Company is adjusting its corporate benefits package by curtailing healthcare coverage for employees’ working spouses. The entertainment conglomerate will exclude spouses of US workers from company medical insurance plans if those spouses have access to healthcare coverage through their own employers. The revised policy will not alter healthcare benefits for other dependent family members.

Article Title: American politicians who once fought for data centers are now trashing them; Texas Senator makes chatbot that tells why state electricity bills are up
Article Text:
A multimillion-dollar AI data centre (Representative image)

Energy cost controversy meets campaign

National political fallout and mounting public resistance

In Ohio, gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy called for a moratorium on approvals until firms guarantee local tax compliance, environmental benchmarks and power concessions.

In Nevada, Democratic candidate Aaron Ford pledged to revoke tax breaks for new developments.

In Pennsylvania, Governor Josh Shapiro issued an executive order enabling state authorities to block projects.

US political figures who previously competed to bring massive artificial intelligence (AI) data hubs to their states are reversing course, are distancing themselves from the facilities as voter frustration grows over surging electricity bills, heavy water usage and fears of job displacement, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal. In Texas, governor Greg Abbott had proclaimed the state the center of AI development following a $40 billion investment from Google. However, Abbott subsequently suspended approvals for roughly 1,800 planned data facilities worth billions of dollars, citing severe demands placed on local power grids and water supplies.The policy shift drew public criticism from President Donald Trump, who defended the facilities as vital economic engines and warned that regions rejecting them risk falling behind.Rising public pushback has turned data centres into a central friction point in regional political contests. For example, state representative Gina Hinojosa, challenging Abbott for the governorship, launched a campaign ad showing a resident asking an AI chatbot why their electricity costs are rising. The chatbot responds by attributing the price hikes to data centres approved under Abbott, highlighting campaign donations he received from AI-linked executives, including Elon Musk.Hinojosa argued that community protections must be written directly into statute rather than relying on voluntary corporate agreements. Similarly, democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed attacked former Representative Mike Rogers over local facility expansion, stating that voters strongly oppose having data centers built near their neighborhoods..Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown challenged Senator Jon Husted over his record on AI infrastructure, labeling him the public face of data centers. In response, Husted stated he has consistently pushed for tech firms to pay local taxes and higher power rates, introducing legislation to enforce stricter operating rules.Concerns over public backlash prompted the National Republican Senatorial Committee to warn candidates in an internal memo that data centres represent a major political liability, cautioning that contenders cannot easily repair the damaged reputation of the infrastructure sector.
Article Summary: US political figures who previously competed to bring massive artificial intelligence (AI) data hubs to their states are reversing course. Voter frustration grows over surging electricity bills, heavy water usage and fears of job displacement. In Texas, governor Greg Abbott had proclaimed the state the center of AI development following a $40 billion investment from Google.

Article Title: What makes September 3 important for international students in the US on F and J visas
Article Text:
US F and J visas: What's at stake and why it is important for international students

The lawsuit and the September 3 hearing

Why the plaintiffs say the rule should be blocked

What happens if the hearing doesn't go the plaintiffs' way

September 3, 2026, has emerged as a pivotal date for international students in the United States on F and J visas, according to multiple reports. On that day, a federal court will hear arguments in a lawsuit challenging a new Department of Homeland Security (DHS) rule that limits how long foreign students and exchange visitors can remain in the country. The rule replaces the long‑standing “duration of status” policy, which allowed students to stay as long as they maintained their academic program, with fixed end dates on visas. The lawsuit, filed by unions, universities, and advocacy groups including the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, argues that the new rule will harm students and institutions alike. Plaintiffs say the change creates uncertainty, increases the risk of inadvertent overstays, and undermines America’s ability to attract global talent. They contend that the “duration of status” framework was essential for flexibility, especially for students pursuing long academic programs or research.International students and exchange visitors have been admitted to the US under the framework known as "duration of status," or D/S for more than four decades. This allows them to stay in the country for as long as they continue making progress in their academic or exchange program and they are not tied to any fixed expiration date.July 17, 2026, DHS published a final rule in which the department replaced the existing system with fixed admission periods. Students who would need more time will now have to apply for a discretionary Extension of Stay through USCIS and also there is no guarantee of approval. Along with this, the rule also imposes restrictions of graduate students from changing their academic programs and bars students from pursuing degrees at the same or a lower level after completing a prior one. The new rule also limits transfers and program changes for undergraduates, and cuts the post-completion grace period for F-1 students from 60 to 30 days. This new rule published by DHS is scheduled to come into effect starting September 15, 2026.On August 18, 2026, a coalition of higher education and labor groups, including NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts, the American Federation of Teachers, and several affiliated unions, filed a lawsuit and a motion for a preliminary injunction in the US District Court for the District of Massachusetts, seeking to block the rule before it takes effect. The case, assigned to District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, is formally titled Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration et al. v. US Department of Homeland Security et al.On August 19, Judge Saylor issued an order setting the briefing schedule: the government's response is due August 31, 2026, with an in-person motion hearing scheduled for September 3, 2026, at 11:00 a.m. in Courtroom 1. That hearing is why the date matters so much for affected students — it's the court's first real opportunity to weigh whether the rule should be paused before its September 15 effective date arrives, leaving a narrow window for a decision either way.The plaintiffs argue the rule is "arbitrary and capricious" under the Administrative Procedure Act, contending that DHS's stated justifications, primarily national security concerns and preventing abuse of the system, rest on scattered anecdotes rather than evidence of any systemic problem with the existing framework. They point out that DHS's own cost-benefit analysis acknowledged billions of dollars in costs while describing the rule's benefits only in vague, qualitative terms.The complaint cites research estimating serious economic fallout: a study referenced in the filing projected that eliminating duration of status could cost the U.S. economy between $72 billion and $145 billion annually within a decade, with related productivity losses potentially reaching $220-439 billion a year by year ten, largely tied to the outsized role international STEM students play in the US economy. The plaintiffs also cite NAFSA research suggesting every three international students enrolled support an additional US job, and note that DHS received nearly 22,000 public comments on the rule, which plaintiffs argue the agency largely dismissed with conclusory responses rather than substantive engagement.Because the rule remains on track to take effect September 15 unless a court intervenes, the September 3 hearing is effectively the last clear checkpoint before the new framework could become active. If Judge Saylor doesn't grant the preliminary injunction, current F-1, J-1 and I visa holders would move from an open-ended "duration of status" framework to fixed admission periods, with all the added uncertainty around extensions, program changes and transfers that the plaintiffs argue the rule introduces. If the injunction is granted, the existing D/S framework would remain in place, at least temporarily, while the broader legal challenge to the rule continues.
Article Summary: September 3, 2026, has emerged as a pivotal date for international students in the United States on F and J visas. On that day, a federal court will hear arguments in a lawsuit challenging a new Department of Homeland Security rule that limits how long foreign students can remain in the country. The rule replaces the long‑standing “duration of status” policy, which allowed students to stay as long as they maintained their academic program.

Article Title: A tech enthusiast spent 3 years testing 351 microSD cards, and 177 have already failed
Article Text:
351 microSD cards, 3 years, 133 petabytes written: 177 are already dead

PNY, Kingston and Delkin top the consumer microSD card rankings

SanDisk and ADATA cards died far sooner than their reputation suggests

High endurance microSD cards did not earn the price premium

What this microSD endurance test cannot tell you

A tech enthusiast has spent three years writing data to microSD cards until they die, and the pile of casualties is now big enough to say something useful about which brands actually survive. Matt Cole, who posts as mikaey00, owns 351 cards covering 111 models from 52 brands. Of those, 177 are dead, 107 are still being tested, and 67 sit on a shelf waiting for a card reader to free up.The scale is hard to picture. Cole's machines have pushed more than 133 petabytes of writes through these cards and finished over 4.6 million program-verify-erase cycles. A card counts as failed when it stops working, makes itself read-only, or shows verification errors across at least half its sectors. He posted the third anniversary update to Reddit's r/DataHoarder, where it pulled close to 6,000 upvotes.The average consumer card in the test has lasted around 10,000 cycles. PNY sits at the top with 10 cards averaging 643 days and 15,700 cycles, and its PRO Elite Prime landed in the top 10 percent for every performance measurement Cole took. Kingston's 12 cards averaged 694 days and roughly 23,500 cycles, with the Canvas Select Plus 32GB still running after nearly the full three years.Delkin's HYPERSPEED 128GB took more data written per card than any other consumer brand and posted the fastest random write speeds in the collection. Lexar and Samsung round out the top five. Amazon Basics 64GB cards have not failed at all after 788 days and 4.2PB written, but Cole left them out of the rankings because Amazon can swap the NAND without changing the product name.The bottom of the list is more surprising. Walmart's onn 32GB cards averaged 40 days and 1,400 cycles. ADATA's Premier 32GB managed 2,350 cycles, Gigastone lasted 114 days on average, and none of Cole's nine Silicon Power cards reached 4,000 cycles. SanDisk gets a dishonorable mention as the biggest brand in the collection. Of 28 consumer cards, only five are still alive, at an average of 384 days and 9,404 cycles.This is the finding buyers should sit with. High endurance cards averaged about 14,000 cycles against 10,000 for consumer models, a gap smaller than the marketing implies, and several performed worse. All three SanDisk High Endurance 64GB cards are dead. Kingston's High Endurance 32GB quit after an average of 143 days. Industrial cards are the real step up at roughly 122,000 cycles, with Kingston's Industrial 8GB hitting 141,600. The oddity is a single Hiksemi NEO 8GB, an ordinary consumer card, which has cleared 143,800 cycles and is still going.Cole runs the project on a shelf of mini PCs and old gaming laptops, including a Beelink Mini-S, five TRIGKEY Green G4 units and an Asus ROG Strix Hero II. He buys most of the cards himself, and rising memory prices are making the hobby expensive.None of this predicts how long a card lasts in a phone or a Steam Deck. It is a torture test. What it does show is that the badge on the packaging is a weaker signal than three years of writes.
Article Summary: PNY, Kingston and Delkin top the consumer microSD card rankings. High endurance cards averaged about 14,000 cycles against 10,000 for consumer models. Amazon Basics 64GB cards have not failed at all after 788 days and 4.2PB written.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Snapchat CEO Evan Spiegel: “It’s not about working harder; it’s about…”
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Evan Spiegel

“It’s not about working harder; it’s about working the system.”

Understanding the meaning behind today’s quote

Why effort is not always the problem

How Evan Spiegel built Snapchat around a different idea

The difference between a shortcut and a better process

What this can mean for a career

How to put the idea into practice

Lessons to learn from Evan Spiegel’s quote

Look for the cause, not just the problem

Do not confuse busyness with progress

Improve processes you use repeatedly

Learn how the system works

Question routines that no longer make sense

Use technology to support better processes

Know when hard work is still necessary

Focus on long-term efficiency, not just immediate results

Find ways to prevent the same problem from returning

Work smarter without treating effort as unimportant

Most people have days when the amount of work seems to grow faster than the time available to finish it. A task takes longer than expected, a simple job turns into several smaller ones, and something that was completed yesterday somehow needs attention again today. The usual response is to keep going. Work a little later, move a little faster and try to clear the next item on the list. Sometimes that is necessary. But there are situations where the problem is not how much effort is being put in. It is the way the work has been arranged. A process may be unnecessarily complicated, a routine may have outlived its purpose, or the same problem may be quietly repeated without anyone questioning why it happens. That is where Evan Spiegel’s observation offers a different way of looking at work and productivity.Working harder is easy to understand. It can mean staying longer, taking on more work, responding more quickly or simply putting greater effort into the same routine.Working the system is different. It means understanding the process around a task and looking for the part that can be improved.If an employee spends an hour every day fixing the same type of mistake, the answer may not be to become better at fixing it. The more useful question could be why the mistake keeps being produced.That distinction matters because individual effort has a limit. A better process can continue producing benefits after the original change has been made.Workplaces tend to reward visible effort. Someone answering emails late at night or completing a large number of tasks can appear highly productive. Less visible is the person who changes a process so those tasks no longer take as long.This can create an odd situation. A worker may become extremely good at dealing with an inefficient system without ever questioning the system itself.There is nothing inherently wrong with hard work. Some jobs demand it, particularly when deadlines are tight or circumstances are difficult. Spiegel’s point is more specific: when a problem repeats, simply increasing effort may not be the most effective response.Evan Spiegel became one of the most recognisable figures in social media after co-founding Snapchat with Bobby Murphy and Reggie Brown while studying at Stanford University.Snapchat took a different approach to online communication. Photos and messages could disappear rather than remain permanently visible, challenging the expectation that everything posted online needed to become part of a lasting digital record.The service grew rapidly and eventually became part of Snap Inc., with Spiegel serving as chief executive. The company expanded its platform through features including Stories, Discover and augmented-reality lenses.“Working the system” can sound as though it means finding a loophole. That is not necessarily the useful interpretation.A shortcut avoids work. A better system changes how the work is performed.Imagine a customer service team receiving the same ten questions every week. Each employee could continue answering them individually. Another approach would be to identify the recurring questions and create information that addresses them before a customer needs to ask.The work has not disappeared. It has moved to a different point in the process, where it can have a wider effect.For someone early in their career, the temptation can be to prove value by accepting more work. Taking responsibility is useful, but becoming the person who constantly fixes the same problems can eventually become limiting.Learning how a workplace operates can be just as valuable as learning how to perform a particular task.Who makes the decision? Where does information get held up? Which tasks are repeated? What requires approval, and does that approval actually change the result?These are practical questions. They can also reveal where someone's time is being consumed.A useful starting point is to watch for repetition.If the same mistake, delay or administrative task appears regularly, stop for a moment before simply dealing with it again. Look at where it begins. Consider who touches the work before it reaches you. Check whether information is being entered more than once. Ask whether a step exists because it is genuinely necessary or because it has simply remained in place.The aim is not to redesign every part of a working day. Sometimes a small adjustment is enough.A template, an automated task, a clearer instruction or a change in who approves something can remove a surprising amount of repeated work.
Article Summary: Evan Spiegel co-founded Snapchat with Bobby Murphy and Reggie Brown. The company expanded its platform through features including Stories, Discover and augmented-reality lenses. Spiegel's quote offers a different way of looking at work and productivity. Do not confuse busyness with progress, and work smarter without treating effort as unimportant.

Article Title: Melinda French Gates who called divorce with Bill Gates one of her life’s most difficult transitions; said: I want to tell everyone to take

Melinda French Gates on divorce and life changes: I want to tell everyone to take

“I want to tell everyone to take time in quiet,”

Mental health and work-life balance

Article Title: Google's former CEO Eric Schmidt is reportedly 'unhappy' with his former boss Sergey Brin; reason is how a $100 million was spent on ...
Article Text:
Why Eric Schmidt is unhappy with Sergey Brin

Where the $100 million is being spent

What is California Proposition 40

Google’s former CEO Eric Schmidt is reportedly unhappy with founder Sergey Brin over how more than $100 million in political contributions is being used in California. The two technology billionaires are backing efforts to defeat Proposition 40, a proposed one-time wealth tax on California residents worth more than $100 million. However, a report says Schmidt has grown frustrated because money raised to fight the tax is also being used against other ballot measures.According to a report by the New York Post, Eric Schmidt has become frustrated with the political coalition led in large part by Sergey Brin after California Democrats endorsed Proposition 40. The former Google CEO and Google co-founder have both donated millions of dollars to Building a Better California, a political organisation fighting the proposed billionaire wealth tax.However, an advisor to Schmidt told Fortune that he was not “irate” over the Democratic Party's endorsement of the measure. The advisor said Schmidt's current political involvement is focused on defeating the billionaire tax. The concern, according to the report, is that money contributed to the campaign is also being used on other political measures.Sergey Brin has provided more than $100 million to Building a Better California, while Schmidt has contributed more than $3 million, according to the report.The group is opposing Proposition 40, but its spending also includes efforts linked to Propositions 41 and 42 and other issues.Proposition 41 would require state audits of programmes funded by new special taxes. Proposition 42 would restrict retroactive taxation and is aimed at countering the proposed wealth tax.The wider use of campaign funds has reportedly become a source of frustration for Schmidt, particularly after California Democrats backed Proposition 40 while rejecting the billionaire-backed alternatives.Proposition 40 is a proposed one-time wealth tax targeting California residents with net worth above $1 billion. If approved, it would impose a 5% tax on the net worth of people who meet the wealth threshold as of January 1, 2026.California's Legislative Analyst's Office has estimated that the measure could affect a few hundred people and potentially generate tens of billions of dollars.The proposal has attracted support from figures including Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Ro Khanna, while several wealthy technology and business leaders are funding efforts to defeat it.
Article Summary: Eric Schmidt and Sergey Brin are backing efforts to defeat Proposition 40, a proposed one-time wealth tax on California residents worth more than $100 million. The former Google CEO and Google co-founder have both donated millions of dollars.
