Article Title: When a fifteen-year-old Michael Dell met Steve Jobs; says: I didn't know that in five years, we will not be...
Article Text:
Michael Dell was 15 when he first saw Steve Jobs speak in Houston in 1980. Five years later, they were friends.

The

Apple II

that Michael Dell took apart before he took notes

What Steve Jobs actually said at that 1980 Houston user group meeting

From Apple fan to Apple's archenemy, and back to friends

Long before Dell became a byword for beige office towers and before Apple became the most valuable company on earth, a fifteen-year-old boy sat in a Houston meeting room and watched a 25-year-old Steve Jobs walk in. The year was 1980. The boy was Michael Dell, four years away from starting a PC business out of a University of Texas dorm room with a thousand dollars and three guys with screwdrivers.In his memoir Play Nice But Win: A CEO's Journey from Founder to Leader, Dell writes that Jobs in person was far more compelling than Jobs in print, and that when he entered the room it felt as though the waters parted. Dell ends the passage with a line that lands harder in hindsight than it could have at the time: he was fifteen and riveted, and he could not have begun to imagine that in five years he and Jobs would be not only colleagues but friends.The obsession started a year earlier. In 1979, Dell begged his parents for an Apple II, which cost around $1,298 then. He unboxed it, admired it, and immediately pulled it apart to see how it worked. His logic was simple. You have to take something apart to understand it. The Apple II obliged, with clearly marked chips and books explaining what each one did.That mix of curiosity and commerce was already there. Dell had been selling Houston Post subscriptions in high school, using marriage licence records to target newlyweds, and made about $18,000 in a year doing it.Jobs was speaking at a moment when Apple was about to go public and was preparing the Apple III, pitched internally as the sequel that would do for the Apple II what the Apple II had done for the Apple I. He spoke about the personal computer, and specifically his personal computer, as something that would revolutionise the world.The metaphor Dell remembered was a transport one. For the capital investment of a passenger train, Jobs said, you could buy a thousand Volkswagens, and the difference was that those thousand people could go where they wanted, when they wanted and with whom they wanted. Computing, in other words, was about to stop being something you queued for.Dell writes that Jobs was saying people would gain the capacity to accomplish the unimaginable. He was fifteen. He believed it.The five years Dell mentions did pass, and the two men did become friends, though the public record mostly remembers the fights. In 1993, Jobs drove to Dell's house in Texas repeatedly to pitch the NeXT operating system for Dell PCs. Dell passed, citing no applications and no customer interest. In 1997, back at Apple, Jobs showed Dell a Dell desktop running Mac OS on Intel silicon and offered to license it. That collapsed over money, because Jobs wanted a royalty on every Dell PC sold, not just the ones running Mac OS.Then came October 6, 1997, when Dell was asked what he would do with Apple and said he would shut it down and return the money to shareholders. Jobs emailed him a one-liner about class. Weeks later he put Dell's face on a keynote screen and told the room Apple was coming after him.Dell now calls the remark stupid and unprofessional. The fifteen-year-old in the Houston meeting room would probably have agreed.
Article Summary: Michael Dell was 15 when he first saw Steve Jobs speak in Houston in 1980. Five years later, they were friends. Dell was four years away from starting a PC business out of a University of Texas dorm room with a thousand dollars and three guys with screwdrivers. The obsession started a year earlier when Dell begged his parents for an Apple II, which cost around $1,298 then.

Article Title: Microsoft to all the students wondering whether it still is worth learning how to code, the answer is: Now…
Article Text:
FILE - The logo of Microsoft is seen outside its French headquarters in Issy-les-Moulineaux, outside Paris on May 13, 2024. (AP Photo/Thibault Camus, File)

AI now writes a big chunk of code at every major tech company

The job has shifted from typing code to judging it

Microsoft Learn, the company's official training and certification arm, dropped a single line on X this week that walks straight into the most anxious question in tech education right now. "If you're wondering whether it's still worth learning how to code, the answer is: Now more than ever." No hedge, no asterisk, no follow-up thread explaining what it really meant.Coming from Microsoft, the timing reads as either reassuring or slightly cheeky, depending on where you sit. This is the same company whose CEO told a room at Meta's LlamaCon that 20% to 30% of the code sitting in Microsoft's own repositories was already "written by software". It is also the company whose CTO, Kevin Scott, has predicted 95% of all code will be AI generated by 2030. So the message to students is not that nothing has changed. It is that the change makes the skill more valuable, not less.The numbers behind the anxiety are real and they keep moving. Nadella noted the AI share was climbing steadily, and that results varied by language, with more progress in Python and less in C++. Google has gone further. Sundar Pichai said in April this year that 75% of all new code at the company is now AI-generated and approved by engineers, up from 50% the previous autumn.Anthropic puts its own figure above 90%.That is the backdrop for every computer science student watching placement season and wondering if they picked the wrong branch. Entry-level hiring has tightened. The "write this simple function" interview question has aged badly. And a lot of loud voices online have taken those two facts and concluded that the whole path is closing.Microsoft's argument, and the one most working engineers make, is narrower than the headline suggests. AI is good at producing code. It is not good at knowing what to build, spotting where something will break in production, or taking responsibility when it does. Somebody has to read the output and decide whether it is right. You cannot do that without knowing how code works.There is also volume to consider. More code is moving through every project than ever before, which means more review, more debugging, more architectural calls. The bottleneck moved. It did not disappear.What has genuinely changed is the shape of the skill. Memorising syntax was never the interesting part, and it is now close to worthless as a differentiator. Understanding systems, reading unfamiliar code, and directing AI tools well are where the leverage sits. Stack Overflow's developer survey found 62% of developers were already using AI coding tools daily, up from 44% the year before. Adoption is not a trend anymore. It is the job.Microsoft Learn, for its part, offers free structured paths in Python, C#, and cloud development, which makes the post part encouragement and part pitch. Both things can be true. For a student staring at a compiler error at 2am, the answer stays the same: keep going.
Article Summary: AI now writes a big chunk of code at every major tech company. The job has shifted from typing code to judging it. Microsoft's CEO said 20% to 30% of the code sitting in Microsoft's own repositories was already "written by software" Google said in April this year that 75% of all new code at the company is now AI-generated.

Article Title: Elon Musk launched a product using the houses from sets of Desperate Housewives as backdrop; 10 years later it is dead, with the company telling ...
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI generated)

Quite end to an ambitious Tesla product

Tesla has pulled the plug on its ambitious Solar Roof line, ending years of production hurdles, customer disputes, and missed rollout targets. First reported by Electrek, the company has notified its network of certified third-party installers that it will no longer supply the integrated solar tiles, shifting its residential energy focus strictly to traditional solar panels, according to people familiar with the matter. For those unaware, the Tesla solar roof was essentially a mini-power plant that happened to look like fancy terra-cotta tiles, or refined slate slabs.Inside the company, leadership ultimately concluded the product was no longer financially viable. The quiet wind-down is already visible on consumer-facing platforms. Tesla’s dedicated Solar Roof landing page now automatically reroutes visitors to its standard panel portal, and references to the product have been stripped from the primary navigation bar on its energy website, leaving only solar panels, Powerwall, and Megapack offerings.The decision brings a quiet end to a marquee product that originally served as the centerpiece of Tesla’s controversial $2.6 billion buyout of SolarCity in 2016. Tesla CEO Elon Musk first showcased the sleek, photovoltaic-embedded glass shingles on a Hollywood backlot. Elon Musk unveiled it in October 2016 on a Hollywood back lot, using homes from the set of Desperate Housewives fitted with the tiles, just weeks before shareholders approved the acquisition.The demo helped convince skeptical investors to absorb the debt-heavy installer, though it later surfaced during shareholder litigation that the demonstration tiles were non-functional prototypes.From the start, the Solar Roof struggled to reconcile Musk’s bold promises with the gritty realities of roofing physics and supply chain economics. Early marketing claimed the system would undercut the cost of a traditional roof combined with standard panels, with early estimates hovering near $22 per square foot. Instead, complex installations and soaring labor costs drove prices drastically higher. A 2021 wave of retroactive price hikes on existing contracts spurred a class-action lawsuit, which Tesla settled for $6 million after some buyers saw their quotes double overnight.Production volume also never matched the rhetoric. Musk once projected Tesla would manufacture and install 1,000 roofs per week by 2020. In practice, installations barely averaged 30 systems a week at their peak. Industry estimates by Wood Mackenzie placed total nationwide deployments at around 3,000 units over seven years—missing Musk’s target by more than 95 percent.After phasing out deployment metrics from financial filings earlier this year, Tesla's pivot back to conventional rooftop panels and residential battery storage is now complete. And as a report in TechCrunch dwells that Tesla’s decision could deal a blow to the idea of a solar roof because if one of the world’s most valuable companies can’t make it work, who possible can?
Article Summary: Tesla has pulled the plug on its ambitious Solar Roof line. The company has notified its network of certified third-party installers that it will no longer supply the integrated solar tiles. The decision brings a quiet end to a marquee product that originally served as the centerpiece of Tesla’s controversial $2.6 billion buyout of SolarCity in 2016.

Article Title: In 2008, Apple opened App Store and built a $100 billion business around it; how court rulings, regulations are now threatening its commission model
Article Text:
Apple’s $100 billion services business faces a new threat as App Store rules begin to erode its commission revenue

“may not earn a commission at all”

App Store commission model faces pressure from court rulings

App Store spending slows as alternative payment rules expand

Apple services business faces regulatory changes across markets

“It would make sense that it starts to show up in the numbers . . . we were surprised that it really wasn’t traceable before,”

“Apple’s premium valuation is predicated on services, and the App Store is really the crown jewel of that,”

“We think the market is going to reprice the durability of the services business take rate.”

Apple has acknowledged for the first time that recent court rulings and regulatory changes are forcing it to loosen control over the App Store, putting pressure on the iPhone maker’s more than $100 billion services business. The changes are also challenging the commission model that has helped Apple generate revenue from apps, subscriptions and digital purchases. The Cupertino-based tech giant reported services revenue and margins below Wall Street expectations in its latest quarter and warned in regulatory filings that iton purchases made through alternative payment systems.The disclosure comes after years of antitrust action in the US, Europe and other markets that have required Apple to allow alternative payment methods and, in some cases, alternative app distribution. Apple launched the App Store in 2008, creating a system in which it collected commissions on digital purchases made through apps. Courts and regulators are now requiring changes to that system, while new research indicates that App Store spending and Apple's commission revenue are slowing in some markets.Apple reported services revenue of $30.7 billion in the June quarter, below analysts' expectations of $31.4 billion, while the division's gross margin of 75.6% also missed forecasts, according to Visible Alpha.Apple shares fell about 9% in the days following the results.The company attributed the services performance to several factors, including foreign exchange movements. Chief financial officer Kevan Parekh also acknowledged that recent App Store changes had affected the business.In a statement to The Financial Times, UBS analyst David Vogt described slowing App Store growth as a “concern”, while Bank of America’s Wamsi Mohan said services revenue of $30.7 billion was a record but still “somewhat weaker than we expected”.The pressure is linked to changes in how developers can collect payments from iPhone users. Apple has traditionally charged commissions of up to 30% on digital purchases and subscriptions made through apps. When users pay through systems outside Apple's payment infrastructure, the company can lose part or all of that commission.A US court injunction won by Epic Games last year forced Apple to allow app developers to direct users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store without charge, bypassing its traditional commission. The USb Supreme Court has agreed to review aspects of the Epic Games case after a judge found Apple had failed to comply with an earlier injunction governing App Store payment rules.New research indicates that the changes are already coinciding with weaker App Store spending in the US. Sensor Tower found US consumer spending through the App Store fell 6% in the second quarter, compared with 9% growth a year earlier. Appfigures estimated that Apple's US commission revenue has contracted 18 per cent so far this year.Sensor Tower said the US slowdown reflected how consumer spending inside the App Store had been “significantly impacted” by the ruling. Global consumer spending through the App Store rose 3 per cent year on year in the June quarter, down from 13 per cent growth a year earlier. The research group also pointed to weaker consumer spending and macroeconomic uncertainty as factors affecting demand.Appfigures found App Store revenue was also contracting in Brazil and Japan after both countries introduced new rules in recent months. The changes in those markets add to regulatory requirements that have already altered Apple's App Store operations elsewhere.Apple argues its tight control of iPhone apps is necessary to protect users. However, regulators in the EU, South Korea and Brazil have required the company to open iPhones to alternative app stores or payment methods, while similar changes are being pursued in the UK and Australia.The European Union has also taken action against Apple's App Store practices. The company was fined €500mn last year over alleged breaches of the Digital Markets Act, a decision Apple is appealing.The combination of regulatory requirements and court decisions means developers in different markets can increasingly use payment and distribution options outside Apple's traditional App Store system. The impact on Apple's revenue depends on the rules in each jurisdiction and how developers and consumers respond to the available alternatives.Apple's latest regulatory filing highlighted the potential financial consequence of those changes, warning that the company “may not earn a commission at all” on purchases made through alternative payment systems.said Nicholas Rodelli, director of legal research at Washington Analysis.he added.
Article Summary: Apple's $100 billion services business faces a new threat as App Store rules begin to erode its commission revenue. Courts and regulators are now requiring changes to that system. New research indicates that App Store spending and Apple's commission revenue are slowing in some markets.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Google co-founder Sergey Brin: “We do lots of stuff. The only way you are going to have success is…” - lesson behind trying, failing and trying again
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Sergey Brin

“We do lots of stuff. The only way you are going to have success is to have lots of failures first.”

Understanding the meaning of the quote

Why doing more can increase the chance of finding something useful

Failure is not the same as progress

Sergey Brin journey to Google

What the quote says about risk

What can be taken from it at work

Lessons learnt from Sergey Brin today’s quote

Not every attempt has to succeed.

Trying different ideas can create better opportunities.

Failure can reveal what needs to change.

Learn from mistakes rather than repeating them.

Do not confuse persistence with repeating the same approach.

Give uncertain ideas room to develop.

Success often follows a long series of unsuccessful attempts.

Judge the quality of the process, not only the final outcome.

Know when to abandon an idea that is no longer working.

Progress rarely follows a straight path.

Experimentation requires patience and flexibility.

The goal is discovery, not failure.

Success rarely looks as straightforward while it is happening as it does in hindsight. A finished product, a successful career or a breakthrough idea can make the journey seem like a series of carefully chosen decisions. In reality, many worthwhile outcomes are shaped by experiments that did not work, ideas that were abandoned and attempts that needed to be started over. That is the thinking behind Sergey Brin ’s observation: “We do lots of stuff. The only way you are going to have success is to have lots of failures first.”The quote speaks to something familiar in everyday life, whether someone is learning a new skill, building a career, starting a business or simply trying to make a difficult decision. Not every attempt will produce the desired result, and some may lead nowhere. But trying creates information that staying still cannot. Brin’s words ultimately offer a practical reminder: progress is often built through repeated attempts, adjustments and the willingness to keep going when the first answer is not the right one.The wording is unusually matter-of-fact. There is no elaborate theory of innovation in it. Brin starts with doing: trying things, building things, testing ideas and moving between possibilities. The second part follows almost as a practical consequence.If many experiments are being attempted, some will not work. That is not necessarily evidence that the process is broken. It can simply be the expected result of exploring several uncertain possibilities.The distinction matters because failure can mean very different things. A project may fail because the technology is not ready, because users do not want it, because the timing is wrong or because a better idea appears. In some cases, the failure provides useful information. In others, it may simply mean that resources were spent on an idea that did not justify continuing.Brin's wording does not suggest that every unsuccessful attempt is valuable in itself. The point is closer to probability. If a person or organisation wants to discover something genuinely useful, it cannot know in advance which experiment will work.Brin and Larry Page's early work offers a useful example of this way of thinking. While studying at Stanford, the two worked on a project examining the structure of the web. Their system, initially called BackRub, used the links between pages as part of a way to determine relevance. That work contributed to the development of PageRank and eventually to Google.The important detail is that Google did not begin as a finished global product. It emerged from academic research, technical experimentation and an attempt to solve a particular problem differently. The route from that early work to a major company was not a single clean leap.That is where Brin's comment becomes more interesting. A culture that allows only ideas with an almost guaranteed chance of success will tend to favour familiar solutions. The safer option can be easier to defend, especially inside a large organisation. But genuinely uncertain ideas are different. Their outcome cannot be known beforehand.Trying more things creates more opportunities for an unexpected result. It also creates more opportunities to discover what should be abandoned.There is an easy misunderstanding in the quote. It would be wrong to read it as saying that failure automatically leads to success.It does not. A failed product can simply be a failed product. Repeating the same mistake without changing the approach does not turn failure into learning. An experiment becomes useful when its result changes what happens next, whether that means refining the idea, changing the question or deciding not to continue.That distinction becomes especially important in technology, where organisations can afford to run multiple experiments at once. Some may be small trials. Others may absorb years of work before being abandoned. The existence of many unsuccessful projects is therefore not, by itself, a sign of good management. What matters is whether an organisation can identify which ideas deserve more time and which do not.Brin's own phrase, “We do lots of stuff”, is revealing in that respect. It suggests volume and variety rather than a romantic attachment to failure.Sergey Mikhaylovich Brin was born in Moscow in 1973 and moved to the United States with his family when he was six. He studied mathematics and computer science at the University of Maryland before going to Stanford University for graduate study in computer science. There he met Larry Page.Their academic interests overlapped around information retrieval and the structure of the web. The paper associated with their early search work described a method for examining the link structure between web documents, reflecting the research problem that eventually became central to Google's search technology.The company itself was founded in 1998. Brin and Page had suspended their graduate studies as the search project developed into a business.When people talk about successful entrepreneurs, attention often goes towards the decisions that turned out to be correct. The unsuccessful decisions tend to disappear from the story. That creates a distorted picture in which the path looks much more deliberate than it probably was.Brin's comment pushes against that version of the story. If an organisation is doing “lots of stuff”, then its record will naturally contain ideas that never become major products. Some will be forgotten. Some may be quietly discontinued. A few will become important.The difficult part is accepting that the successful outcome cannot always be identified at the beginning.For a company, this can also affect how teams are evaluated. If employees are punished every time an uncertain project fails, they have an incentive to avoid uncertain projects. They may choose work that is easier to justify rather than work that could produce something genuinely different. That does not mean there should be no accountability. It means the quality of the decision and the quality of the experiment can matter separately from its eventual outcome.For an individual, the practical reading of Brin's quote is fairly simple: not every attempt needs to become a finished success.A writer may produce several weak ideas before finding the right angle. A designer may reject multiple versions of a concept. A business owner may test a service that attracts little interest. A researcher can spend months pursuing a hypothesis that does not hold up. The useful question after each attempt is what has been established.Sometimes the answer is substantial. Sometimes it is merely that one particular route is not worth taking again. Both can save time later.There is also a difference between experimenting and constantly changing direction. Doing many things does not mean doing everything at once without discipline. Experiments still need a question, a reason for being tested and some way of deciding what happens afterwards.
Article Summary: Google co-founder Sergey Brin's quote of the day. He said: “The only way you are going to have success is to have lots of failures first” The quote speaks to something familiar in everyday life, whether learning a new skill, building a career, starting a business or simply trying to make a difficult decision.

Article Title: One of world’s most popular festivals has a ‘privacy warning’ for smart AI glasses wearers
Article Text:
Clarifying the rules on consent and wearable tech

The growing controversy over discreet cameras

Amid the concerns over breach of privacy by smart spectacles such as Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses, Burning Man 2026 has officially permitted them but the event organisers are delivering a warning directive to attendees: respect personal boundaries and obtain explicit consent before recording anyone. Citing the official Burning Man 2026 Survival Guide, Business Insider reports that attendees must ask for and receive permission from every person captured within their recording frame, including individuals in the background as well as direct subjects, before operating cellphones, digital cameras, or smart eyewear. The mandate covers both private moments and artistic installations across the desert gathering.A spokesperson for the Burning Man Project explained to the publication that while the festival’s baseline privacy and consent standards are longstanding, the 2026 documentation was updated to explicitly name smart eyewear due to rapid advancements in wearable tech. The spokesperson emphasised that the organisation prioritises attendee privacy and insists that all media recording practices respect personal boundaries and the collective experience across Black Rock City.The policy shift highlights how smart frames are moving into the cultural mainstream while sparking discussions around individual privacy.Hardware like Meta’s Ray-Ban and Oakley AI glasses resemble everyday frames while concealing built-in microphones, speakers, artificial intelligence assistants and high-definition cameras. While fans praise the ability to capture first-person video hands-free without reaching for a smartphone, the hidden cameras have sparked major privacy backlash.The devices feature a white LED indicator that illuminates during recording, but bystanders frequently overlook it. Some users have deliberately placed stickers over the light or altered the hardware to disable it, leading Meta to issue a mandatory software patch to prevent tampering.Meta committed to scrubbing harassing footage recorded covertly on its hardware, though reports have uncovered numerous violating videos that stayed active online for weeks after the enforcement was announced. Meta stated it has removed thousands of improper posts and took down additional videos once alerted.Burning Man 2026 takes place from August 31 through September 7 in Nevada’s Black Rock Desert.
Article Summary: Burning Man 2026 has officially permitted smart eyewear. But the event organisers are delivering a warning directive to attendees: respect personal boundaries and obtain explicit consent before recording anyone. The mandate covers both private moments and artistic installations across the desert gathering.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Andrew Carnegie: No man will make a great leader who wants to do it all himself or to get all the credit for doing it
Article Text:
Andrew Carnegie

What Andrew Carnegie's quote implies

Why the quote still matters

Andrew Carnegie's life and self-motivation

Legendary industrialist Andrew Carnegie is remembered for his thoughts on leadership, teamwork and success. One of his widely cited quotes focuses on an important lesson for anyone trying to lead: “No man will make a great leader who wants to do it all himself or to get all the credit for doing it. ” The quote highlights the importance of trusting others, sharing responsibility and giving credit to a team. Its message remains relevant in workplaces and organisations, where effective leadership often depends on collaboration rather than individual achievement.Andrew Carnegie’s quote suggests that leadership is not about doing every task alone or taking credit for every success. A person may have strong skills, but leading others also requires the ability to trust a team and allow people to contribute.The quote also points to the importance of recognising the efforts of others. A leader who takes all the credit can weaken teamwork, while one who acknowledges contributions can build trust and encourage people to perform better.The quote has a simple lesson for leaders: You don’t have to do it all yourself to be successful. Today, leaders in the workplace often have to delegate, trust their teams and give credit for individual contributions.Sharing responsibility allows employees to use their strengths to help the organization achieve a shared purpose.Carnegie’s words therefore continue to be relevant for managers, business leaders and anyone working as part of a team.Andrew Carnegie was a Scottish-American industrialist who made his career in the steel industry in the late 19th century. Carnegie was born in Dunfermline, Scotland, in 1835, and immigrated with his family to the United States in 1848, working as a boy in a factory before moving through jobs in telegraphy and railroads. He later founded the Carnegie Steel Company, which was sold in 1901 to become part of US Steel.Often, his rise from factory worker to one of the world’s largest steel operations is mentioned alongside his thoughts on ambition, persistence, and self-driven effort. In the latter part of his life, Carnegie devoted much of his wealth to philanthropy, funding libraries, educational institutions and research organisations throughout the United States and other countries.His perspective is often referenced in discussions about workplace performance, education, and goal-setting, where consistent action and personal discipline are seen as important drivers of long-term progress and effective skill application.
Article Summary: Andrew Carnegie’s quote suggests that leadership is not about doing every task alone or taking credit for every success. The quote highlights the importance of trusting others, sharing responsibility and giving credit to a team. Its message remains relevant in workplaces and organisations where effective leadership often depends on collaboration rather than individual achievement.

Article Title: Meta sued by former manager claiming was fired for refusing to sign immigration letter for a Chinese engineer; here's all lawsuit blames the company for
Article Text:
The dispute began in 2024 when Meta and outside immigration lawyers were preparing an I-140 petition for an employee in Tillinghast’s product design organisation

Why former Meta manager is suing the company

Former manager claims Meta retaliated against him

Lawsuit accuses Meta of unequal immigration support

Meta Platforms is reportedly facing a lawsuit from a former product design manager who claims he was fired after refusing to sign an immigration support letter for a Chinese engineer. James Tillinghast filed the lawsuit on August 17 in a US District Court in New Jersey. He alleges that the letter overstated the employee’s work and that he raised concerns about how Meta provided immigration assistance to some workers. The lawsuit claims the company retaliated against him after he refused to support statements he believed were inaccurate. It accuses Meta of providing immigration support more often to some Chinese national employees than to similarly placed workers from other countries.According to the lawsuit, the dispute began in 2024 when Meta and outside immigration lawyers were preparing an I-140 petition for an employee in Tillinghast’s product design organisation. The petition sought an EB-2 National Interest Waiver, which can allow certain foreign workers to seek permanent residency in the US without a specific job offer and the usual labour certification requirement.A proposed managerial reference letter allegedly credited the employee with generating about $638 million in additional advertising revenue.It also described the worker as developing artificial intelligence tools and taking on wider leadership responsibilities. James Tillinghast claims that parts of the letter did not accurately describe the employee’s actual responsibilities.Tillinghast says engineering teams carried out much of the technical work that was attributed to the employee. He claims he discussed his concerns with Meta’s immigration legal team and worked with the employee to revise the letter.However, according to the complaint, Tillinghast eventually refused to sign statements that he believed he could not personally support.The lawsuit alleges that after he raised his concerns, his manager, Bolan Wang, provided or signed a replacement letter for the immigration petition.Tillinghast claims Meta then revoked his access to internal systems around August 29, 2024. His employment was formally ended on September 30.James Tillinghast alleges that Meta did not identify a performance improvement plan, written warning or documented performance issue when his employment ended. He claims the company later blamed his dismissal on poor performance, but argues that this explanation was a pretext for retaliation over his objections.The lawsuit names both Meta Platforms and Wang as defendants.The former manager also makes a separate allegation about Meta’s immigration assistance. According to the complaint, Meta provided company-coordinated immigration support more frequently to certain Chinese national employees than to similarly situated employees from other countries.The alleged assistance included access to immigration lawyers, help preparing and reviewing petition documents and support in obtaining managerial reference letters.Tillinghast claims Meta did not apply neutral and consistent criteria when providing these benefits.The lawsuit argues that immigration support was an employment-related benefit and that his objections to what he believed was unequal treatment were protected under New Jersey law.
Article Summary: James Tillinghast filed the lawsuit on August 17 in a US District Court in New Jersey. He alleges that the letter overstated the employee’s work and that he raised concerns about how Meta provided immigration assistance to some workers. The lawsuit claims the company retaliated against him after he refused to support statements he believed were inaccurate.

Article Title: Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro takes a hard line against data centers; says: I have heard loud and clear from the good people of Pennsylvania that ...
Article Text:
Pennsylvania data center projects face new restrictions (Representative image)

“heard loud and clear from the good people of Pennsylvania”

“I’ve heard loud and clear from the good people of Pennsylvania as I’ve traveled our commonwealth, and I’m here to say today that we will not be bullied by these developers,”

“We will not be bulldozed by the lawyers working for these big tech companies. That will not happen in the commonwealth. We have a long history in Pennsylvania of industry running roughshod over our communities to make a buck — that stops with me.”

Pennsylvania data center projects face new restrictions

Josh Shapiro changes position on data center development

“Part of the challenge here is how quickly the industry has moved,”

“And so the opposition, I think, has moved just as quickly,”

“Now it’s coming upon us and certainly others to bring the facts and the data to bear but also be out there and demonstrate how this industry invests in the communities for the long term.”

Data center proposals draw criticism from Pennsylvania governor

“I’m a hell no on that project,”

“I’m a hell no on many other projects.”

“speculators”

“They’re threatening to fundamentally change the character of our communities,

Pennsylvania data center rules put local officials in charge

“Again, there are only about five projects that have even received permits to go forward,”

“The problem is there’s 100 projects or so that are wreaking havoc on our communities that are never going to be built.

What we’re doing today is taking concrete action to listen to the voices of the people, to put local leaders back in charge of their communities and to make very, very clear what the rules of the road are to be able to do business here in Pennsylvania.”

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has ordered new restrictions on data center projects in the state. Under the new order, companies will be required to obtain local approval for such projects, while data center developments will also be removed from Pennsylvania’s fast-track permitting program. Announcing the executive order this week, Shapiro said he hadand would not allow developers or technology companies to push projects through communities without local consent.Shapiro said.Under the executive order, data center projects must first receive approval from local officials. Developers will also have to sign a legally binding order committing to requirements Shapiro outlined in February, including paying for their own power, hiring locally, maintaining transparency with local governments and meeting water-conservation standards.Shapiro also said data center projects would no longer qualify for Pennsylvania’s fast-track permitting program. The order further bars nondisclosure agreements for data center projects in the state, increasing the amount of information that developers will have to make available during the approval process.The governor said the changes were prompted by what he described as an increase in speculative proposals. After the state announced two major Amazon-backed data center projects last year, Shapiro said Pennsylvania had received a large number of additional proposals, including projects he said were unlikely to be built.Shapiro's latest position represents a change from his earlier approach to data center development. Earlier this year, while introducing guidelines for the industry, he argued that Pennsylvania should play a role in the competition for artificial intelligence development and said data centers were an important part of the AI economy.He also stressed at the time that the state needed to be selective about which projects it pursued. Since then, opposition to data center developments has grown in Pennsylvania, with residents and local officials raising concerns about electricity costs, water use, environmental effects and changes to the character of communities.Josh Shapiro said conversations with residents had influenced his position.Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, said in a recent interview.he added.During his remarks, Shapiro specifically criticised data center proposals that he said had faced opposition from residents and local officials. He pointed to a project in Montgomery County, where he lives, and accused a developer of attempting to push the proposal forward despite local resistance.he said, adding,Shapiro also said Pennsylvania’s divided Legislature had not moved forward with new data center regulations, leaving him to use executive authority to establish requirements for future projects.He described some developers asand accused them of putting pressure on township officials and residents.” he said, adding that the lack of legislative progress on passing new regulations for data center development — Pennsylvania’s Legislature is under split control — left him no choice but to move on the executive order.Following his announcement, Shapiro was asked whether he regretted Pennsylvania’s earlier approach to data center development. He said only a small number of projects had received permits, while many more proposals had generated opposition despite having little prospect of being constructed.he said.The new requirements mean future data center developers in Pennsylvania will have to secure local approval, meet the governor’s conditions on power, employment and water use, and operate outside the state’s fast-track permitting process. The changes come as Shapiro faces re-election this fall and as data center development becomes a growing issue in state and local elections across the US.
Article Summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has ordered new restrictions on data center projects in the state. Under the new order, companies will be required to obtain local approval for such projects. Data center developments will also be removed from Pennsylvania’s fast-track permitting program.

Article Title: GitHub CTO apologises to developers after one of the biggest outages; admits: Since April, monthly commits have doubled, this shows pressure on our systems, but it is no excuse for outages
Article Text:
What caused the GitHub outage : an autoscaling policy watching the wrong thing

Why GitHub’s own growth has become its biggest reliability problem

GitHub has apologised for the outage that took its platform down for 7 hours and 47 minutes on August 17, and the explanation is unusually blunt. Nobody pushed bad code. Nobody fumbled a configuration change. The platform simply ran out of room.In a blog post published on August 20, Vlad Fedorov wrote that traffic hit a new peak and a critical infrastructure component in GitHub’s Central US data centre failed to scale with it. Authentication buckled first, and the pressure spread outward through github.com, Actions, APIs, pull requests, issues and Copilot. “If you were trying to ship software that day, we let you down,” the post reads.The root cause analysis points at an Istio sidecar reaching its concurrency limit while the autoscaling policy monitored the host service instead. Load balancers in Central US saturated. A latent retry bug in Visual Studio Code then amplified traffic to a single internal endpoint by roughly 10 times, which is what kept the Copilot Token Service down long after everything else came back. Engineers cut gateway retries and began rejecting inbound Copilot token requests with HTTP 403 responses.Scraping attacks on codeload endpoints made recovery messier still.At the worst of it, GitHub’s status page reported error rates near 20 percent for web and API traffic, and around 50 percent for archive and raw repository downloads. Most services recovered by 1636 UTC, Actions by 1803 UTC, and the Copilot Token Service only at 2102 UTC.Fedorov’s numbers explain the strain better than any apology. Monthly commits have climbed from 1.4 billion in April to 2.9 billion now. GitHub has added more than 3 million CPU cores and 120 petabytes of high-speed storage, and installed as much hardware as available power allowed in existing data centres. Azure now carries about 58 percent of platform load, up from 12 percent in May, and handles half of all Git operations.What comes next is a fix list: consistent retry limits, retry budgets and variable timeouts across service-to-service calls, a review of lower-priority CPU and memory alerts, and a new architecture that scales read capacity linearly with the number of readers, rolling out first to the largest monorepos.The timing is awkward. This was GitHub’s second incident in August, after an Actions failure on August 6. Cursor announced an early beta of its Origin Code Hosting product while GitHub was still dark. CloudBees CEO Moritz Plassnig wrote on LinkedIn that GitHub will not be the default choice going forward, and that the ecosystem is heading somewhere more bifurcated.
Article Summary: GitHub has apologised for the outage that took its platform down for 7 hours and 47 minutes on August 17. The root cause analysis points at an Istio sidecar reaching its concurrency limit while the autoscaling policy monitored the host service instead. GitHub has added more than 3 million CPU cores and 120 petabytes of high-speed storage.

Article Title: Mayor Zohran Mamdani's Office decides to skip in-person appearance at City Council meeting for which council members complied 'pages and pages' of questions about rollout of 'second house tax' in the
Article Text:
Zohran Mamdani

Why Zohran Mamdani 's Office stayed away

Council members demand answers

Defending the release of property data

How the controversy started

Residents report confusion and privacy concerns

A pending lawsuit

The city's response and next steps

New York City Mayor administration opted not to attend Tuesday’s (August 25) City Council hearing on the rollout of the pied‑à‑terre tax, submitting a written memo instead, according to a report by Business Insider. Finance Commissioner Richard Lee said ongoing litigation prevented him from appearing in person, though he pledged to testify after the lawsuit is resolved. The levy, passed in May, imposes a progressive surcharge on non‑primary residences valued at least $5 million, and condos or co‑ops worth $1 million or more. In late July, the Department of Finance (DOF) sent letters to 17,000 addresses and published valuations for nearly 960,000 properties, sparking confusion and privacy concerns. Some residents reported receiving letters for their primary homes, while others criticized the release of property records.As reported by Business Insider, in the memo Department of Finance Commissioner Richard Lee detailed that the pending and active litigation prevented him from appearing at the hearing directly. He further added that he would have welcomed the chance to filed council members’ questions in person.Lee also noted that the Administration had asked the Council to postpone the hearing until the litigation was resolved, a request the Council declined. He said he would be prepared and willing to testify in person after August 31.Council Member Gale Brewer said her office has been “bombarded” with constituent complaints and compiled “pages and pages” of questions for the Mayor’s Office. The Council had requested an in‑person briefing, but the administration declined, citing the pending lawsuit.A central point of contention has been the DOF's release of home values and addresses ahead of the levy. In his written testimony, Lee maintained that this practice is standard, stating that the City's assessment roll is "highly accessible to the public, and it has been for many years," and pushing back directly on any suggestion otherwise. He pointed out that this property data has long been available as a searchable database on both the DOF website and NYC Open Data, with online archives dating back to fiscal year 2009, and that assessment rolls have been required to be published annually in New York for well over a century.The uproar began in late July, after the NYC Department of Finance sent letters to roughly 17,000 addresses identified as potential pied-à-terre properties based on property values and internal records. The DOF also published a broader list of more than 900,000 properties and their valuations across the city.Lee clarified in his testimony that this supplemental roll does not itself determine which properties are actually subject to the surcharge; rather, it exists to identify relevant properties and give owners a basis to challenge their valuations. Homeowners have until September 18, an extended deadline, to demonstrate that their property doesn't qualify for the tax before it could begin appearing on bills starting in 2027.Some New York residents said on social media that they mistakenly received letters intended for non-primary residences despite the property in question being their primary home, while others said they felt their privacy had been compromised by the DOF's broader records release. Council Member Gail Brewer, who represents Manhattan's Upper West Side, told Business Insider that her office has been inundated with concerned constituents in recent weeks, and that she and fellow council members had compiled extensive lists of questions about the rollout that they hoped the Mayor's Office would address.Separately, a lawsuit filed by three residents based in Manhattan and Staten Island is pending, with a court date scheduled for August 31. According to court documents, the plaintiffs are seeking emergency relief, arguing that the DOF's records release caused widespread confusion and invited unwanted scrutiny of homeowners' personal information. Their attorney, Randy Mastro, said hundreds of thousands of New York City homeowners had been drawn into a process they should never have been part of in the first place.The city has hired two dozen staffers specifically to field resident questions about the tax and assist with appeals. The policy itself, passed in May, imposes a progressive levy on non-primary homes valued by the DOF at $5 million or more, and on condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more. Deputy Press Secretary Matt Rauschenbach previously told Business Insider that the Law Department is prepared to vigorously defend the city against the lawsuit, and said the roughly $500 million a year the levy is expected to raise would help fund cleaner parks, safer streets, and other public investments across the city.In his written testimony, Lee also detailed the broader implementation process, noting that the surcharge was authorized under state legislation passed as part of New York's 2026/2027 budget on May 28, 2026, with rules formally adopted by DOF on July 14 following a public comment period that included a hearing held July 9. He emphasized that the initial determination letters sent to around 17,000 property owners represent only a small subset of the roughly 960,000 properties listed on the supplemental roll, and stressed that receiving a letter does not constitute a tax bill, only a preliminary determination that owners can challenge by submitting proof of primary residency or by contesting their property's valuation directly with the Tax Commission.The Department of Finance (DOF) intends to expand its outreach efforts by engaging with senior centers, hosting community meetings, and leveraging 311 services. Additionally, the department plans to coordinate directly with co-op and condo boards, property managers, and elected officials to ensure homeowners have access to clear information and a transparent process for challenging any inaccurate tax determinations.
Article Summary: New York City Mayor administration opted not to attend Tuesday's City Council hearing on the rollout of the pied‑à‑terre tax. Finance Commissioner Richard Lee said ongoing litigation prevented him from appearing in person, though he pledged to testify after the lawsuit is resolved. The levy, passed in May, imposes a progressive surcharge on non‑primary residences valued at least $5 million, and condos or co‑ops worth $1 million or more.

Article Title: Most companies across America laying off employees seemingly have a new slogan: Not being replaced by ...
Article Text:
Messaging around AI-led job cuts is changing in America

From bragging AI-led job cuts to backtracking on messaging

Public anxiety growing around employment

The new ‘job cuts’ messaging: ‘Reshaping, not replacing’

CEOs across corporate America have previously highlighted the rapid advance of artificial intelligence (AI) by noting how many human workers the technology could replace. Today, amid growing public concern and rising economic nervousness, company leaders are adopting far more cautious language, avoiding direct links between workforce reductions and automation. According to a report by Axios, communications teams are caught between conflicting priorities: shareholders demand measurable evidence that heavy AI spending is boosting margins, while employees push back against being discarded in favour of automated software.The corporate narrative around generative automation has shifted dramatically over the past two years. In 2024, Klarna announced that its AI assistant took over the workload of 700 full-time support workers, with CEO Sebastian Siemiatkowski boasting about doing “much more with less.”Similarly, last year, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff stated that AI helped trim customer support roles from 9,000 to roughly 5,000 because fewer people were required. Moreover, in May, Coinbase laid off about 700 staff members as CEO Brian Armstrong outlined plans to rebuild operations around smaller, “AI-native” teams.Following AI-led job cuts, executive rhetoric has become a reputational risk as worker anxiety continues to climb.Citing a CBS News/YouGov survey of 2,287 adults conducted between August 12–14 revealed that 61% of Americans expect AI to decrease overall economic opportunities, compared to only 21% who anticipate growth.Meanwhile, a Pew Research study found that 73% of Americans under the age of 30 believe AI will eliminate jobs over the next twenty years. Further reporting by consultancy Challenger, Gray & Christmas, suggests that AI remained the single most cited factor behind American job cuts in July for the fifth consecutive month, accounting for roughly 113,000 announced cuts, which is nearly 24% of all nationwide layoffs this year.Rather than framing layoffs around headcount displacement, corporate leaders now use careful phrasing to argue that automation is merely changing how work gets done. For example, Microsoft’s chief people officer Amy Coleman explicitly described 4,800 recent role eliminations as “not being replaced by AI,” while noting that the tools are redefining daily tasks.Similarly, Etsy CEO Kruti Patel Goyal clarified that cutting 220 jobs was not driven by AI and Patreon CEO Jack Conte maintained that a 20% workforce reduction was not rooted in replacing human staff, despite AI fundamentally changing platform workflows.
Article Summary: CEOs across corporate America have previously highlighted how many human workers the technology could replace. Today, amid growing public concern and rising economic nervousness, company leaders are adopting far more cautious language. Microsoft’s chief people officer Amy Coleman explicitly described 4,800 recent role eliminations as “not being replaced by AI,” while noting that the tools are redefining daily tasks.

Article Title: SIM Card rules changing: What you can do and cannot do after August 24
Article Text:
New SIM card rules come into effect from August 24

How the new SIM verification system will work

What happens if you try to get an extra SIM

SIM card limit in India

Most parts of India: 9 mobile connections

Jammu and Kashmir: 6 mobile connections

Assam: 6 mobile connections

North-East: 6 mobile connections

SIM card rules are set to change from August 24, with telecom companies being asked to stop people from getting mobile connections beyond the permitted limit. In a circular, the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) has directed telecom operators to identify customers who already have the maximum number of SIM cards allowed in their name. Such customers will be informed that they cannot get another mobile connection. The new system will initially work on a post-facto basis, but operators have been told to move to real-time checks by November 30.Under the existing DoT rules, an individual can have a maximum of nine mobile connections in their name across telecom operators and licensed service areas in India. However, the limit is lower in some regions. Customers in Jammu and Kashmir, Assam and the North-East can have up to six mobile connections.From August 24, telecom companies will have to take steps to identify customers trying to get another SIM after reaching this limit. The DoT has directed operators to tell such customers that they have already reached the maximum number of mobile connections allowed and that a new connection cannot be issued.The new system will use subscriber photographs to help telecom companies identify people who have already reached the permitted SIM limit.The DoT will make representative images of subscribers who have reached the maximum limit available on the Digital Intelligence Platform (DIP) from August 23.Telecom operators will have to download these images every day and use them to identify customers attempting to obtain additional mobile connections.The DoT said, “From 24.8.2026 onward, TSPs shall take appropriate technical and organisational measures to identify each subscriber who seeks to obtain mobile connections beyond the prescribed limit…”Initially, the system will work on a post-facto basis. This means telecom operators can carry out the verification after a new connection has been enrolled. If a connection is activated beyond the permitted limit during a day, it will have to be immediately suspended until the issue is resolved.The government has also asked telecom companies to move towards a real-time system so that excess connections can be identified and stopped during the enrolment and activation process.Here is the maximum number of mobile connections an individual can hold:Customers also have to declare the mobile connections already held in their name across different telecom operators and licensed service areas in the Customer Application Form (CAF).
Article Summary: New SIM card rules come into effect from August 24. Telecom companies will have to identify customers trying to get another SIM. They will be told that they have already reached the maximum number of connections allowed. The new system will initially work on a post-facto basis, but operators have been told to move to real-time checks.
